sermon:
## The Dark and Lovely Want
*On the goodness of a desire the poem refuses to silence*

**Text:** Song of Songs 1:1-2:7 · **Supporting:** Genesis 2:25 · Proverbs 30:18-19 · Psalm 42:1-2 · Ephesians 5:31-32

The church has been embarrassed by this book for a very long time. We have allegorized it the moment it opened its mouth, because a woman saying out loud that she wants a man's kisses was more than the sanctuary could bear. So we made the kisses into doctrine and the body into a diagram, and we missed the thing the Spirit actually inspired. A woman in love, saying so, without apology. Solomon called it "the Song of Songs" (Song of Songs 1:1), not a song, the song, the best of them, the superlative the Hebrew reserves for the holy of holies. The most exalted poem Israel possessed was a poem about wanting a person. We should sit down under that before we say another word.

**She speaks first, and she speaks her wanting**
The Song does not open with achievement. It opens with appetite. "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your love is better than wine" (Song of Songs 1:2). She has not earned him. She has not finished a course of moral preparation. She wants, and the wanting is the first word, and the poem treats that first word as good. Notice who is talking. It is the woman. In a world that handed women very little voice, the Spirit gives her the opening line, and the line is desire. She is not being acted upon. She is the speaking subject, naming her own longing in the first person, and the canon lets her keep the microphone for most of the book. Then she says the thing the room least expects: "I am very dark, but lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem... Do not gaze at me because I am dark, because the sun has looked upon me" (Song of Songs 1:5-6). She knows the field has burned her brown. Her brothers were angry, she was made keeper of the vineyards, her own vineyard she could not keep. She names her own deficiency in the same breath she claims her own beauty. She is not pretending to be more than she is, and she is not collapsing into less than she is. She wants, and she is honest, and both are allowed to stand. This is what Eden was before the fall split want from goodness, "the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed" (Genesis 2:25). Nakedness without shame. Wanting without apology. That is the country this poem remembers, and the whole Song is, in part, the long work of getting us back to it.

**The poem honors desire and refuses to satisfy it yet**
Here is the discipline of the Song, and it is a holy discipline. It blesses the longing and it does not rush to consummate it. The lovers praise one another. He calls her beautiful and likens her to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots; she calls him a sachet of myrrh that lies between her breasts. The language is unhurried, lush, in no rush to arrive. And then, at the very moment the desire has built to its highest pitch, the woman turns to the daughters of Jerusalem and lays down a charge: "I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases" (Song of Songs 2:7). She will say it again in chapter three and again in chapter eight, three times this refrain, a hand laid on the rushing thing. She has just said her wanting is real and her bed is real. And in the same breath she says: not yet, not before its time, do not pry this open prematurely. The poem holds desire and patience together, which the culture around us cannot do. Our age says a desire felt is a desire owed, that to wait is to repress, that the only sin is the unmet appetite. Proverbs already knew better, that the way of a man with a woman is among the things "too wonderful" to grab at and dissect and explain away (Proverbs 30:18-19). Wonder is not for seizing. It is for receiving in its hour. The Song honors the want precisely by refusing to cheapen it with haste. The patience is not the enemy of the desire. The patience is the proof the desire is being taken seriously.

**We have called the wanting sin, and God called it the field He made us to stand in**
I have preached a Christianity that was secretly relieved this book was hard to read. It let me keep desire at arm's length, label it suspect, treat the body as a problem to be managed rather than a gift to be governed. And I have watched what that teaching does in a marriage, in a young believer told to feel ashamed of his own longing, in a man who never learned the difference between desire and idolatry and so killed them both together and called the killing holiness. We were taught that the spiritual move is to want less. The Song says the spiritual move is to want rightly, and at the right time, toward the right person, with your whole self and no shame. The same God who breathed out this poem is the God who put into the psalmist the cry, "As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God. My soul thirsts for God, for the living God" (Psalm 42:1-2). He is not nervous about longing. He is the author of it. The thirst in the body and the thirst in the soul were lit at the same fire. And this is why Paul could take a man and a woman becoming one flesh and say of it, "This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church" (Ephesians 5:31-32). The longing of the bride for the bridegroom is not a distraction from the gospel. It is a rehearsal of it. Christ does not want His church a little. He wanted her better than wine, better than His own life, dark from the field and lovely in His eyes, and the field that burned her was her own sin, and He looked at her anyway and called her lovely, and He said so on a cross. If you have been ashamed of your wanting, the cross does not shame it. It shows you what wanting at full volume looks like when it is finally holy.

Desire is not the enemy.

## He Came Over the Mountains
*On a love that leaps the distance and does not lose what it seeks*

**Text:** Song of Songs 2:8-3:11 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 52:7 · Luke 15:4 · John 10:3-4 · Revelation 19:7

Waiting is the part nobody preaches. We will preach arrival, the wedding, the embrace. We skip the winter where she lies in the dark not knowing if he is coming, because winter does not make a good sermon illustration and we are addicted to resolution. And the Song will not let us skip it, because the whole weight of the second movement is the moment she hears something before she sees anything. A sound on the hills. Before there is a face, there is a sound.

**The voice arrives before the face**
"The voice of my beloved. Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills" (Song of Songs 2:8). She does not say I see him. She says I hear him, and what she hears is motion toward her. He is not strolling. He is leaping. He is "like a gazelle or a young stag" (Song of Songs 2:9), all speed and intent, and the mountains that stood between them are not obstacles he negotiates around; they are obstacles he clears. Then he arrives at her wall, he looks through the lattice, and he speaks, and his first word is a summons out of the cold: "Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away, for behold, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. The flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come" (Song of Songs 2:10-12). This is the gospel cadence, and the prophets knew it long before the lovers sang it. "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace" (Isaiah 52:7). The good news comes over mountains. It comes as a voice before it comes as a sight. It calls the cold thing up into the spring. And notice the woman who waits in winter does not manufacture the spring. She does not generate the thaw by the strength of her longing. She hears it approaching, and she is told to rise. The command and the comfort are the same word: arise. The one who could not make the winter end is summoned out of it by the one who can.

**The night of searching and the certainty underneath it**
And then the poem does something honest, because real love is not one unbroken spring. After the leaping comes a night she cannot find him. "On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but found him not" (Song of Songs 3:1). She rises, she goes out into the city, through the streets and squares, she asks the watchmen who patrol the dark, "Have you seen him whom my soul loves?" (Song of Songs 3:3). The searching is real and it is dark and it is full of strangers who cannot help her. But mark the turn, and mark how fast it comes. "Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go" (Song of Songs 3:4). The seeking that felt like loss was never loss. He was being found the whole time she was searching. This is the secret the Lord Himself spoke over a single sheep, that the shepherd "goes after the one that is lost, until he finds it" (Luke 15:4). Until. Not in case. Until. The sheep that wanders is not, in the end, the searcher; it is the sought. And the searching woman of chapter three discovers that the longing in her was answered by a coming toward her that she did not start and could not stop. He who seeks does not lose what he seeks. That is not romantic flattery dressed up as theology. That is the architecture of how God keeps His own, and it is the only reason any of us is held tonight.

**We are the ones who waited in the cold, and He came anyway, and the wedding is His doing**
The movement ends not with longing but with a procession. The king comes up from the wilderness in his litter, columns of smoke, sixty mighty men around it, and the daughters of Zion are told to go out and look on King Solomon "on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart" (Song of Songs 3:11). It ends in a wedding. And I have to tell you where I have stood on this, because the place I stood was wrong. I have preached as though the burden were on the waiting bride to keep the flame, to seek hard enough, to long with enough purity to deserve the coming. And that is a quiet heresy, because it makes the wedding her achievement instead of his pursuit, and it leaves the anxious soul forever measuring whether she has wanted Him well enough to earn His arrival. The shepherd of John 10 "calls his own sheep by name and leads them out... and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice" (John 10:3-4). The voice came first. The naming came first. He came over the mountains while she was still in winter, and her job was not to summon Him but to rise when she heard Him. The whole New Testament gathers this up into one image and will not let it go: "the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready" (Revelation 19:7). The Lamb comes. He leaps the distance sin put between us, and the distance was not a hill, it was a grave, and He clears it, leaping over the mountain of His own death, and He calls the cold thing up into spring, and He does not lose what He seeks. If you are in the winter tonight, if your bed is dark and you do not know whether He is coming, hear the order of the verbs. The voice before the face. The coming before the wedding. Him before you, always Him before you.

He came over the mountains.

## A Garden With a Wall
*On the exclusive belonging that makes delight whole instead of small*

**Text:** Song of Songs 4:1-5:1 · **Supporting:** Genesis 2:24 · Malachi 2:14 · 1 Corinthians 7:4 · 2 Corinthians 11:2

Our age has a creed about love, and the creed is that boundaries shrink it. Keep your options open. Belong to no one fully and you will have more. Commitment is the cage and freedom is the open field. The Song walks straight into that creed on the wedding night and tells it the opposite, and it tells it with a wall and a lock and a sealed spring, and it calls all of that not a prison but a paradise.

**He praises her whole, head to foot, and withholds nothing**
The bridegroom looks at his bride and he does not glance. He surveys. "Behold, you are beautiful, my love, behold, you are beautiful" (Song of Songs 4:1), and then he goes down the whole length of her, her eyes like doves, her hair, her teeth, her lips like a scarlet thread, her neck like the tower of David, line after deliberate line, slow, unembarrassed, until he gathers it all up and says, "You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you" (Song of Songs 4:7). No flaw. Not because she has none, she told us in chapter one the sun had darkened her and her own vineyard went unkept, but because love that has bound itself to one person stops auditing. This is the delight of a covenant, not the appraisal of a marketplace. In the marketplace you compare; you hold the thing in your hand and weigh it against everything you did not buy, and so nothing you have ever satisfies you. In the covenant you cherish; you have chosen, the choosing is finished, and now you are free to find this one person altogether beautiful. The man who has given himself to one woman is free in a way the man with options will never feel, because he is no longer running every other face against hers. That is the freedom the open-option culture can never reach. It is always comparing, and so it is never at rest, and it has the gall to call its restlessness freedom.

**The garden is locked, and that is exactly why it is glorious**
Then comes the image the whole movement turns on, and it is an image our ears are trained to hear backward. "A garden locked is my sister, my bride, a spring locked, a fountain sealed" (Song of Songs 4:12). Locked. Sealed. To us that sounds like deprivation, like something shut away from life and use. The Song means the exact opposite. The garden is glorious because it is for one. A public fountain is trampled; a sealed spring is sweet. And watch what the bride does with the wall around her, this is the hinge of the whole text. She does not resent it. She opens it. "Awake, O north wind... Let my beloved come to his garden, and eat its choicest fruits" (Song of Songs 4:16). The very enclosure she could have called a cage, she throws open to him, and to him alone, and he answers her invitation with quiet completeness: "I came to my garden, my sister, my bride, I gathered my myrrh with my spice" (Song of Songs 5:1). And then a voice, many take it as the voice of God Himself blessing the union, says, "Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love" (Song of Songs 5:1). Heaven is not embarrassed by this garden. Heaven toasts it. This is one flesh exactly as Eden defined it, where "a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh" (Genesis 2:24). Hold fast. Cleave. Leave all others and bind to one. The exclusivity is not the wall around the joy keeping it small; it is the soil the joy grows out of. A spring poured out to everyone waters nothing deeply. A spring sealed for one becomes a garden a man can lose himself in for fifty years.

**We have wanted the delight without the wall, and lost both, and called it freedom**
I have counseled men who wanted the garden and despised the lock, and I will not stand up here and pretend I watched them from a safe distance. I have been the man who, in his own heart, wanted the warmth of belonging without the cost of being wholly bound, who wanted to be cherished while keeping a door cracked for the comparison. We treat fidelity as the tax we grudgingly pay on pleasure rather than the very thing that makes pleasure whole. And God, through the prophet Malachi, names exactly what that does to a covenant. The Lord is "witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant" (Malachi 2:14). By covenant. Not by feeling, not by convenience, not by however long the chemistry holds, by a wall both of you built and both of you swore to keep. Paul takes the locked garden straight into the marriage bed without a flinch: "the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does" (1 Corinthians 7:4). Wholly given over. Wholly possessed. The lock works both ways and it is mutual and it is total. And then Paul lifts the whole image off the page and sets it on Christ and the church: "I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:2). The church is a garden enclosed. Christ does not want a bride who keeps her options open with other lords, who hedges her devotion, who loves Him while leaving a door cracked for the idols. He wanted her sealed, for Himself, set apart by a wall He built with His own blood. And that exclusivity is not the church's confinement. It is her glory and her safety. The love that died for you is not a love that is content to share you.

A garden for one.

## The Door She Opened Too Late
*On a love proven not in the ease of having but in the cost of seeking again*

**Text:** Song of Songs 5:2-6:13 · **Supporting:** Hosea 2:14-15 · Luke 22:61-62 · John 21:17 · Lamentations 3:31-32

The wedding does not end the story, and any preacher who stops at the wedding has read neither marriage nor the gospel. Chapter four was the garden opened, the delight blessed, the wine of love poured out. Chapter five opens with a closed door and a woman who would not get up in time. The Song knows what we would rather not admit. The danger to deep love is not always a rival. Sometimes the danger is comfort.

**She heard him knock and she did not rise**
This is the most painfully honest passage in the book. "I slept, but my heart was awake. A sound. My beloved is knocking" (Song of Songs 5:2). He is at the door in the night, dew on his head, asking to come in, calling her his sister, his love, his dove, his perfect one. And she, already in bed, already settled, already warm, answers with the excuse every long marriage knows by heart: "I had put off my garment; how could I put it on? I had bathed my feet; how could I soil them?" (Song of Songs 5:3). It is not refusal exactly. It is delay. It is the small, reasonable, fatal reluctance to be inconvenienced by the one you love. By the time her heart catches up to her hands, by the time desire moves her to the door and she opens, "my beloved had turned and gone" (Song of Songs 5:6). She had him. She delayed. He withdrew. "My soul failed me when he spoke." This is not the failure of a bad marriage. This is the failure that lives inside a true one, the slow comfort that treats the beloved as a given, that assumes the door can be opened any time you finally feel like rising, that lets the knock go unanswered because the bed is warm and the feet are clean and surely he will wait. Love that is securely had can be quietly neglected. The Song refuses to pretend otherwise, and it puts the neglect in the mouth of the bride herself, not some outsider.

**She rises into a city that wounds her, and still she seeks**
What she does next is the heart of the whole movement and the reason this is a love story and not a tragedy. She does not roll over and go back to sleep. She gets up into the dark and goes looking, and the city that once held her safe is now cruel to her. "The watchmen found me as they went about in the city; they beat me, they bruised me, they took away my veil" (Song of Songs 5:7). The seeking costs her blood. The same watchmen she once asked for help now wound her. And here is the line that separates covenant love from convenient love, the line we should not be able to read without trembling. She keeps seeking anyway. She turns to the daughters of Jerusalem and says, "if you find my beloved, that you tell him I am sick with love" (Song of Songs 5:8). And when they ask her, almost mocking, what makes this beloved better than any other, she does not curse the one who turned and left. She praises him, head to foot, the way he had praised her, his head finest gold, his eyes like doves, his arms rods of gold, his appearance like Lebanon, until she lands on the verdict of her own wounded heart: "He is altogether desirable. This is my beloved and this is my friend" (Song of Songs 5:16). The seeking is bloodied and the seeking is worshipful at the same time. This is precisely the country the prophet Hosea was sent into, where God says of His unfaithful bride, "I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her... and make the Valley of Achor a door of hope" (Hosea 2:14-15). The valley of trouble, Achor means trouble, becomes the door of hope. The wound of the search becomes the way back. And by chapter six he is found, and he speaks of her again, and union is restored. But it was restored through the bruising, not around it.

**We are the ones who let the knock go unanswered, and grace is that the seeking is not over**
I know which person I am in this text, and if you are honest, so do you. I am the one who has had the Beloved at the door and stayed in bed because rising would cost me a warmth I had carefully arranged. I have let the knock go because answering it was inconvenient to the comfortable life I built around having Him. I have treated grace as a possession instead of a Person at the door. And here is the gospel buried alive in a love poem. When Peter denied Him three times and "the Lord turned and looked at Peter," Peter "went out and wept bitterly" (Luke 22:61-62), there is the door closed by his own mouth, the warm fire of denial and the cold dawn after. But the story did not end at the closed door. By another charcoal fire the risen Christ came seeking, and asked three times, "Simon, son of John, do you love me?", one question for each denial, and gave Peter back the very thing he had thrown away, and said, "Feed my sheep" (John 21:17). The seeking went both directions. The one who had been failed went searching for the one who failed Him. This is why the prophet, sitting in the literal rubble of a burned city, could still write, "the Lord will not cast off forever, but, though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love" (Lamentations 3:31-32). If you have neglected Him, if the bed was warm and the knock went unanswered and now the room feels empty and you are sure it is your own fault, do not lie back down. Rise into the dark and seek Him. The bruises of the watchmen are not the end of the story. The end of the story is that He was seeking you the whole time you thought you had finally lost Him.

She rose and sought him.

## Wholly His
*On a belonging so complete it is not the loss of the self but the home of it*

**Text:** Song of Songs 7:1-8:4 · **Supporting:** Genesis 2:23 · Jeremiah 31:33 · 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 · 1 John 4:19

There is a fear underneath every deep love, and we rarely say it out loud because saying it out loud makes us sound ungrateful for the love we have. The fear is that to be fully given to another is to be finally erased. That to belong entirely to someone is to disappear into them, that the price of being wholly loved is that there is no more you. The Song arrives, in its fifth movement, at a single sentence that takes that fear apart from the inside and hands it back to us harmless.

**The settled language of mutual possession**
By now the lovers have moved through longing and waiting, through the wedding night and the garden, through the closed door and the bruising search and the finding. They have a history now. And out of that history they land here: "I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me" (Song of Songs 7:10). Hear what is different from the way she spoke at the beginning. Back in chapter two she said, "My beloved is mine, and I am his" (Song of Songs 2:16), her claim first, then her surrender. By chapter seven the order has quietly reversed: I am his, and his desire is for me. She names her belonging to him before she names anything she possesses of him. This is not a woman diminished by the years. This is a woman so settled in being loved that she can lead with being possessed, because she has learned across the whole poem that his desire is the safest place she will ever stand. The grasping anxiety of early love is gone. She is not clutching. She invites him out to the villages, to lodge among the vineyards, to see whether the vines have budded, and she tells him she has stored up for him "all choice fruits, new as well as old, which I have laid up for you, O my beloved" (Song of Songs 7:13). New and old. The fresh delights and the long-kept ones, all of it saved for him. Mutual possession, spoken at last without a tremor, without a hedge, without fear.

**To be wholly given is the place the self was made for, not the place it is lost**
The world hears "I am my beloved's" and flinches, because the world has a doctrine of the self that says you are most yourself when you belong to no one. Autonomy is the highest good; commitment is the compromise; the unattached soul is the free soul. The Song says the opposite, and it does not argue the point so much as simply sing it true. The self was made for belonging and finds itself there, not in spite of belonging but by means of it. This is the logic of Eden itself, where the man, given the woman, breaks into the first poetry in Scripture and says, "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh" (Genesis 2:23). At last. As though Adam, surrounded by a perfect garden and walking with God in the cool of the day, were somehow not yet complete until there was a someone to whom he wholly belonged. Belonging did not subtract from Adam. It finished him. And the deepest belonging God ever promised His people follows the very same shape. The new covenant is not God keeping a respectful distance to protect our independence. It is God saying, "I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people" (Jeremiah 31:33). My people. Wholly His, written on, possessed all the way down to the heart. That is not the erasure of Israel. That is Israel finally home. The self is not destroyed by total belonging to the right one. The self that belongs to no one is the self that is actually lost, wandering, keeping every door open and walking through none of them.

**We guard ourselves from being possessed, and so we are never at home, and Christ bought the right to possess us whole**
I have watched people, and I have to confess I have been the person, who keep one room of the self locked against everyone, against the spouse, against the friend, against God Himself, in the name of staying free. The marriage is real but there is a sealed room. The faith is real but there is a withheld corner. And that locked room is not freedom. It is exile with the lights on. We call it independence; Scripture calls it homelessness. Paul says the thing the modern ear can hardly stand to hear: "you are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body" (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). Not your own. The exact wholly-given language the bride speaks to her husband, Paul speaks of the believer to Christ, and Paul does not present it as bondage to be endured but as the ground of glory, of a body finally given over to the One who made it and bought it. And how does anyone ever come to say "I am my beloved's" without the old fear in their throat? There is only one way, and the apostle names it in five words: "We love because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19). She can lead with belonging because he led with desire. The church can say "I am wholly His" without terror only because He said it first, and He said it not in a poem but on a cross, where He gave Himself over entirely, withholding no room, locking no door, so that He could have her entirely. He was wholly given before He ever asked you to be. The belonging He asks of you is the belonging He has already paid for in full. To be wholly His is not to lose yourself in some great erasing love. It is, at the long last of the whole poem, to come home.

Wholly his, and wholly mine.

## A Love Many Waters Could Not Drown
*On the verdict the whole Song was singing toward, a love that holds when everything gives way*

**Text:** Song of Songs 8:5-14 · **Supporting:** Romans 8:38-39 · 1 Corinthians 13:7 · Ezekiel 16:8 · Revelation 19:6-7

Every poem is reaching for a final line, and the Song has been reaching for this one from the first kiss. After the longing and the waiting, after the wedding and the garden, after the door that closed and the search that bled and the belonging spoken at last without fear, the whole book gathers itself up and speaks its verdict. And the verdict is not about feeling. The poem that opened with desire does not close with desire. It closes with strength. With what holds. With what cannot be put out.

**The seal, the death, the grave**
She comes up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved, and she asks for the one thing that turns a feeling into a covenant. "Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm" (Song of Songs 8:6). A seal in the ancient world was ownership and permanence and identity pressed into wax that could not afterward be undone. To be a seal on the heart was to be carried at the center; to be a seal on the arm was to be the strength behind every deed. She asks to be made permanent, fixed, not a passing season of warmth but a mark that does not lift. And then comes the sentence the entire poem was built across eight chapters to carry: "for love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave" (Song of Songs 8:6). Strong as death. Notice the Song does not reach for a flower or a sunrise or any soft thing to measure love against. It reaches for death and the grave, the two powers in this world that take everyone and lose no one, that no wealth bribes and no army defeats. The Song says love belongs in that weight class. Love does not yield to death; it matches death's own grip, hand for hand. And the jealousy named here is not the petty insecurity we hear in the word. It is covenant jealousy, the holy refusal to share what has been wholly given, fierce and unyielding as the grave that will not loosen its hold on what it has taken.

**The fire many waters cannot quench**
Then the image turns from the grave to fire, and to the source of the fire. Love's "flashes are flashes of fire, the very flame of the LORD. Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it" (Song of Songs 8:6-7). The very flame of the LORD, and this is the one place in the entire book where the divine Name itself rises to the surface, as if the Song cannot pronounce its final verdict on love without telling us at last where this fire was lit. It is not merely human warmth. It is a coal off the altar of heaven. And the floods cannot drown it. Bring everything against it, every wound, every winter, every absence, every cruel watchman in the dark, every door opened a moment too late, let the flood rise to the throat, and the fire does not go out. Then the Song adds its final disclaimer, the one that strips love out of the marketplace forever: "If a man offered for love all the wealth of his house, he would be utterly despised" (Song of Songs 8:7). It cannot be bought. It is not for sale and it does not respond to price. This is the same love the apostle Paul defined when he wrote that love "bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things" (1 Corinthians 13:7). Endures all things. It is, by its very design, the love that is still standing when the flood has finished and gone back down.

**This is a love we cannot generate and a love that has already been spoken over us in blood**
Here is where I have to stop preaching at you and stand in the indictment myself. I cannot produce a love this strong. Neither can you. Set this verse beside my actual loving, conditional, easily tired, quick to withdraw the moment the door becomes inconvenient, and the comparison is not flattering, it is humiliating. Strong as death? My love is not reliably strong as a single hard Tuesday afternoon. And that, precisely, is why this final movement does not leave us with a command to love harder, to dig deeper, to manufacture more fire from the cold hearth of our own hearts. It tells us where the fire is from. The very flame of the LORD. And the God who is that flame found His people exactly the way Ezekiel describes, a child cast out in an open field, kicking in its own blood, unwanted and unwashed, and He passed by, and "I spread the corner of my garment over you and covered your nakedness; I made my vow to you and entered into a covenant with you, declares the Lord GOD, and you became mine" (Ezekiel 16:8). You became mine. He sealed it with a vow when there was nothing in us to want. And when many waters finally rose, and they rose, the whole flood of every sin the church ever committed against her Lord, the full weight of the grave itself, He went down under those waters on a cross, and the floods did not drown His love, because three days later He came up out of the grave that was supposed to keep Him, with His bride still sealed upon His heart. This is why Paul can stake his whole existence on it without a hedge: "neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers... nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:38-39). Many waters tried. The grave tried. The Song knew the verdict centuries before the cross went and proved it true. And so the poem that began with one woman's quiet longing ends as the longing of all creation answered, the day the whole multitude roars like many waters, "For the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready" (Revelation 19:6-7). The same many waters that could not quench the love now roar the wedding it survived to reach. The love you could not generate has already been spoken over you, in blood, strong as death, and the grave could not keep it, and the flood could not drown it, and neither can you.

Many waters cannot quench it.
